match.reason: The bank point covers global sourcing and scale gains, but the new point is about technology choices for customer data and the cost and risk of dealing with overseas suppliers and retailers, which is a different idea.

rejected.title: Technology and global issues in setting up
card: A new business can use technology to build a customer database: a stored list of customer details, such as names, emails and past orders. It helps the business contact customers and see what they buy.
A database brings a choice about data. The business must collect only what it needs, keep it safe and follow Australian privacy law. A data breach can harm customers and the business's reputation.
A business can also deal with overseas suppliers or sell to overseas retailers. This can lower the cost of goods or reach more customers.
Global dealings bring risks. Exchange rates can change the price paid, shipping can be slow or costly, and it is harder to check a supplier's quality and standards.
rejected.remember: Technology and global dealings can help a new business, but each brings choices about data, cost and risk.

a.q: Priya opens an online shop in Geelong and stores her customers' names, emails and orders. Which choice does this database mainly bring?
opts: How to keep the customer data safe and use it lawfully
How to avoid the effect of exchange rate changes
How to set the steps for handling a staff complaint
How to pick a supplier with the lowest delivery price
a.why: A customer database holds personal details, so the business must keep them safe and follow privacy law. Exchange rates matter when dealing overseas, not for a local database.
a.clue: Think about what is stored in the database.

b.q: Sam's Melbourne café switches to an overseas supplier of coffee machines because the price is 20% lower. Which risk should Sam weigh before agreeing?
opts: The cost in Australian dollars may rise if the rate moves
The supplier will be sure to deliver late
The lower price shows the machines are poor quality
Australian privacy law will apply to the machines
b.why: If the Australian dollar falls, the same overseas price costs more in Australian dollars, which can cancel the saving. A low price does not prove poor quality, and late delivery is possible but not certain.
b.clue: The supplier is paid in another country's money.

version.title: Technology and global issues in setting up
card: A customer database is a stored record of customer details, such as names, emails and past orders. Software lets a new business build one to contact customers and see what they buy.
Holding personal details brings choices about data: what to collect, how to store it securely and how to protect customers' privacy. A data breach can harm customers and the business's reputation.
Dealing with overseas suppliers or retailers can cut the cost of stock or reach more customers. Shipping adds time and cost, and quality is harder to check from far away.
Overseas deals are often priced in another currency, so exchange rates add risk. If a buyer's currency falls against the Australian dollar, each sale there earns fewer dollars.
version.remember: A database and overseas deals can help a new business, but each brings choices about data, cost and risk.

a.q: Lena starts an online plant shop in Ballarat and saves each buyer's name, address and order history. What choice does this mainly raise for her?
opts: How to protect the personal details she holds
How to cope when exchange rates move suddenly
How to set the steps her staff follow each day
How to compare the prices of two plant growers
a.why: A customer database holds personal details, so Lena has to decide how to keep them secure and private. Exchange rates matter when trading overseas, not when storing local customers' details.
a.clue: Think about what the database holds.

b.q: Jack's Bendigo clothing label agrees to sell through a retailer in Japan and will be paid in yen. Which statement about this deal is correct?
opts: A fall in the yen could cut what each sale earns
A rise in the yen could cut what each sale earns
Shipping to Japan adds no extra time or cost
Selling overseas lowers what his stock costs
b.why: Jack is paid in yen, so he changes it into Australian dollars. If the yen falls against the dollar, each sale converts to fewer dollars. A rising yen would do the opposite and earn him more.
b.clue: He has to change the yen into Australian dollars.

a.best: How to protect the personal details she holds

b.best: A fall in the yen could cut what each sale earns
